theme: Coaching as the Core Manager Behavior
title: The Practicum
tagline: The GROW practicum: live coaching triads, real topics, and the beat-by-beat debrief.
description: An in-person, navigator-led practicum for Vanderbilt managers: coach a real brought topic in live triads, rotate through coach, coachee, and observer, and debrief the four beats to find where your coaching stalls.
heroLead: You know the four beats: goal, reality, options, will. Knowing them is not the skill. In this room you coach a real topic in front of an observer, sit in every seat of the triad, and find out exactly which beat stalls when it is your turn to ask.
objectives: Coach a real brought topic through all four beats with an observer tracking each one
Play coachee and observer well: bring a real topic, and track beats instead of solving problems
Name the beat that stalls on you and leave with the question that unsticks it
missionTie: Manager behavior is where a century-defining university becomes real for its people. A room of managers coaching each other out loud is Exceptional Core Operations practicing itself, one triad at a time.
goalLead: Goal 2 measures demonstrated leader behavior, and coaching sits at the center of the standard. Today it gets demonstrated for real: witnessed, debriefed, and repeated until the stall points show.

agenda.d: Coach, coachee, observer: three seats, three jobs, and a real topic each person actually brought.
Live coaching through the four beats, with rotation so every manager sits in every seat.
Observer notes on the table: where each talk stalled, and the question that would have moved it.

manifesto: Nobody coaches well in theory. Find your stalled beat and practice that.

sections.headline: Three seats, three jobs.
sections.lead: A triad is a coaching gym. The coach runs the four beats. The coachee brings a real work topic they want movement on. The observer tracks the beats, not the problem. Every seat teaches, and the observer often learns most: they hear what the coach cannot.
sections.group: Form triads across tables, ideally with managers you rarely work with. Coachees: pick the real topic you brought, work-sized, roles only, and say it in one sentence.

card.text: Track the beats, not the problem. Note the moment the coach told instead of asked, the beat that got skipped or rushed, and the exact question that moved something. The topic is a prop; the coaching is the work.

interaction.context: Soon this room becomes a dozen live coaching conversations at once, and the most tempting seat to waste is the observer's. The problem being coached will be interesting; a better idea for solving it will occur to you. Write down beats and questions instead. Your debrief is the coach's mirror.
interaction.discuss: When you have watched a great coach or a great question at work, what did it actually sound like? And what do you expect to be hardest about staying out of the problem?
interaction.q: Mid-round, the observer spots the coach handing over a solution. The observer's job is...

opts.t: Step in and model the better question live
opts.why: A second coach collapses the round. The coachee now has an audience of fixers, and the coach loses the rep they came for.

opts.t: Note the moment, the beat, and what a question would have been
opts.why: Exactly. Written observation, delivered in the debrief, is what turns one conversation into three people's learning.

opts.t: Judge whether the handed-over solution was any good
opts.why: The problem is a prop. Whether the fix was clever is beside the point; the point is who did the thinking.

sections.headline: Real topics make it real practice.
sections.lead: Rounds run on brought topics, not scripts, because the beats only get tested by something true. Coach: goal first, reality before options, their options before yours, will with a date. Coachee: answer honestly. Rotate seats after each round until everyone has coached.
sections.group: Run the round: coach and coachee work the four beats while the observer writes. Then rotate one seat and start the next round with a fresh topic.

interaction.intro: Every coaching talk stalls somewhere. Hear each snippet the observers heard and name the stalled beat.
labels: Goal stall: a fuzzy want, accepted
Reality stall: options came too early
Will stall: it ended without a date
interaction.passMsg: Your ear is calibrated. Whatever your observer says next, you will recognize the stall they name.
interaction.failMsg: Close. The tells: a want nobody sharpened, options before anyone said what is true, and a warm ending with no commitment attached.

items.q: Coachee: 'I just want the project to be less chaotic.' Coach: 'Great. So what could you try?'
items.why: The want was fog and the coach accepted it. One more question, what would less chaotic actually look like, gives the whole talk a target.

items.q: Moments in, coach and coachee are trading fixes for a problem neither has actually described yet.
items.why: Options born before reality are guesses. What have you tried, what happened, what is in the way: that ground makes options worth having.

items.q: The round ends warmly: 'Lots of good ideas here. Let's definitely keep talking about this.'
items.why: Pleasant, and nothing will happen. Which one will you do, and by when? The named action with a date is the part that survives the meeting.

sections.headline: The stall is the finding.
sections.lead: Observers report: where the talk stalled, the moment telling replaced asking, the question that moved something. Then the room compares. Most managers stall on the same beat every time, and naming yours is the most useful thing you take from this room.
sections.group: In your triad: observer reports from notes, beat by beat. Coach names their stall in one sentence and writes the question they will bring to the next real talk.

interaction.intro: You are coaching and the round stalls. Choose your recovery for the two commonest stalls.

opts.t: Fill it fast with your best suggestion.
opts.coach: The silence was the thinking. Your suggestion just took it back, and the coachee learns that waiting you out produces answers.

opts.t: Rephrase the question right away, more simply.
opts.coach: Kindly meant, and it resets their thinking just as it was forming. Rephrase only when they ask you to.

opts.t: Let it sit, then: 'take your time. What else?'
opts.coach: Held silence plus a small invitation. What comes after the pause is usually the truest thing said in the round.

slots.key: Their plan is worse than yours

opts.t: Swap it out for your plan, gently.
opts.coach: The thinking just moved back to your head. They leave with a better plan and less ownership, which loses the quarter to win the week.

opts.t: Ask leading questions until they guess your plan.
opts.coach: A quiz with one right answer is telling in disguise, and they can feel it. Real questions have answers you do not already hold.

opts.t: Name the gap you see, then ask what they would do about it.
opts.coach: Honest and still theirs. You contributed what you see; the plan, and the fixing of it, stays in their hands with a date attached.

heads.strong: The stall broke and the thinking stayed theirs. That is the whole craft, witnessed.
heads.mid: Movement, mostly yours. The conversation went somewhere; the coachee walked out carrying your map.
heads.weak: The stall won. The talk ended tidy, owned by nobody, and the same stuck comes back next week.

reactions.strong: At your next real 1:1, the silence arrives and you recognize it as progress instead of failure. The question you wrote in this room is the one you ask.
reactions.mid: Your coachees keep leaving with good plans that quietly belong to you. The stalled beat is still stalling; the observer's note tells you where.
reactions.weak: A month on, the same topics rotate back through your 1:1s, raw as ever. The fix is reps: the beat you avoid is the beat to practice next.

recap.q: The observer's job during a live round is...
recap.why: Beats, not the problem. The written moments, told or asked, skipped or held, are what make the debrief a mirror instead of a critique.

recap.q: The talk jumps straight from the want to a list of fixes. What got skipped?
opts: Reality: what is true and already tried
recap.why: Options built before reality are guesses. What have you tried, what happened, what is in the way: that ground is what makes options worth choosing between.

recap.q: A coaching talk ends with 'let's keep talking about this.' What is missing?
opts: A named action with a date
recap.why: The will beat is the part that survives the meeting. Which one will you do, and by when, said in their words, is what makes the talk a change.

recapMsgs.high: Calibrated. Now go find your stall in a real conversation.
recapMsgs.mid: Solid. Rerun the stalls in your head, then build your card.
recapMsgs.low: Walk the four beats once more before you commit.

capstone.headline: One stalled beat. One question. One real talk.
capstone.lead: Name the beat your observer caught and the question that unsticks it. Role only for anyone you mention; nothing you type is saved or sent.
capstone.whoLabel: Your stalled beat, and the question you will bring to the next real coaching talk.
capstone.whoPlaceholder: e.g. will; 'which of these will you do, and by when?'

practices.name: The stalled-beat rep
practices.move: Open your next 1:1 with the question you wrote for your stalled beat, and let the silence do its work.

practices.name: The full round
practices.move: Run all four beats on the next real stuck a team member brings: goal, reality, options, will, their words, their date.

practices.name: The triad rematch
practices.move: Reconvene your triad from today for one more round each, new topics, same observer discipline.

whens.out: The rep happens at your next 1:1, the question ready before the meeting starts.
The rep happens this week, in whichever conversation hands you a stuck first.
The rep happens within two weeks, with the triad rematch booked today so it cannot slide.

capstone.evidenceRow: Afterward, one line: what did they figure out that you did not have to tell them?

closing.headline: Practiced in a room. Used in a 1:1.
closing.lead: You coached for real, in front of witnesses, and you know your stall. This month's weekly sessions keep feeding the same behavior: the moment, the record, and the listening.
closing.nextTag: Your one next step · This week
closing.nextTitle: Run the rep on your card
closing.nextBody: Bring the question to a real conversation and let the beats do the rest. Your observer's note is the coaching plan; the triad rematch keeps it honest.
closing.brandline: Coach out loud. Stall, learn, repeat.

facilitator.audience: Vanderbilt people managers and team leads, in person. Triads need space: tables of six that split into two triads work best, with room noise expected and welcome; navigators float between triads. Works from nine managers upward; every topic is real and every exercise runs roles only, never names.
facilitator.pulse: Seven days out, send the pulse: 'Did the rep on your card happen? What did the person figure out without being told? Which beat is your next practice?' Count of completed reps feeds the manager-standard behavior metric for the month.

s1.title: Set the triads
s1.purpose: Form working triads, load the three jobs, and get every coachee to a real, work-sized, roles-only topic said in one sentence.
s1.say: This room runs on a simple bet: coaching is a physical skill, and physical skills need reps in front of someone who is watching. So, triads. The coach runs the four beats. The coachee brings a real topic, something actually stuck this month, work-sized, roles only. The observer has the strangest and best job: track the beats, not the problem. You will sit in all three seats before we are done.
facilitate: Form triads across tables so nobody coaches a close colleague; direct traffic until every triad has three seats filled.

Show the observer's rule card and the In the room context; run the discussion on what great questions sound like. Then hand out the printed observer checklists, one per triad: the four beats, told versus asked, and a line for the question that moved something.
Coachees write their topic in one sentence and read it to the triad. Navigators sweep for topics that are really grievances about named people; help reshape them toward the coachee's own next move.

ask.q: Coachees, is your topic real enough to matter and small enough to coach?
expect: Real project stucks and priority tangles
A few too-big topics, like a whole reorg
A few too-safe ones picked to stay comfortable
ask.respond: Too big shrinks to its next decision; too safe swaps for the thing you actually thought of first. Real topics are what make the reps count.

s1.debrief: Three seats, three jobs, real topics on the table. The observer tracks beats, and the checklist is their script.
s1.watchFor: Triads forming from adjacent seats and existing teams. Break them up cheerfully; strangers make braver coachees and more honest observers.
s1.coreNote: Core: form triads by numbering off instead of choice, and skip the discussion; the checklist walkthrough carries the observer teaching.

s2.title: Run the rounds
s2.purpose: Run rotating live rounds through the four beats with observers writing, until every manager has coached once.
s2.say: Round one starts now. Coaches: goal before options, reality before options, their options before yours, and a will with a date. Coachees: honest answers, including the uncomfortable ones. Observers: pen moving, mouth closed. When the round lands its will, rotate one seat and the next topic comes out. The room will get loud. Loud is what practice sounds like.
facilitate: Call the start and let the noise build; resist the urge to hush the room. Navigators kneel in with triads whose coach is lecturing and whisper one question stem: what have you tried?
Between rounds, run Call the stall on learner devices; the snippets calibrate every observer's ear for the next round.

Rotate until everyone has coached once. If a triad's round dies early, the observer reports immediately and the same pair reruns from the stalled beat; that rerun is often the best coaching of the day.

ask.q: Coaches, what surprised you about being watched?
expect: The urge to fix got louder
Silence felt endless with an observer there
The checklist made me hear my own questions
ask.respond: All of that is the practicum working. The observer's presence turns habits you cannot hear into notes you can read, which is the entire point of doing this out loud.

s2.debrief: Every manager coached, every talk got witnessed, and the stalls are now on paper. The debrief spends them.
s2.watchFor: Coaches interviewing forever to avoid the will beat. Signal triads to land the round: which one will you do, and by when, is how a round ends.
s2.coreNote: Core: two rounds instead of three; whoever has not coached becomes first coach in the triad rematch, and say so out loud.

s3.title: Debrief the beats
s3.purpose: Turn observer notes into named stalls and one prepared question per manager, then set up the take-home rep.
s3.say: Now the part you cannot get alone at your desk: the mirror. Observers, report from your notes, kindly and specifically: where the talk stalled, the moment telling replaced asking, and the question that moved something. Coaches, listen for the pattern; most of us stall in the same place every time. Then we practice the two commonest recoveries, because knowing your stall is half, and having the next move is the other half.
facilitate: Triad debriefs first, observer speaking from the checklist. Then chart the room: each triad calls out its stalls and you tally goal, reality, options, will on the flip chart. Name the crowded column; the room's shape is always a teaching moment.
Run Unstick the beat on learner devices; it rehearses the recoveries for the two stalls every column shares.
Each coach writes their stalled beat and their unsticking question on a card; that pair rides straight into the capstone.

ask.q: What does our flip chart say about this room?
expect: A pile-up on will, in most rooms
Goal stalls from politely accepting fog
ask.respond: Whatever the crowded column is, that is the room's collective rep. Individually, trust your observer over your self-image; the note is the truth.

s3.debrief: A named stall, a written question, and a recovery for the silence and the better-plan trap. That is a complete practicum takeaway.
s3.watchFor: Debriefs drifting into re-solving the coachee's problem. Pull them back to the beats; the topic was a prop and the coaching is the work.
s3.coreNote: Core: skip the room tally; triad debriefs only, and the stalled beat goes straight onto the capstone card.

facilitator.capstoneSay: Your observer gave you a finding; now it becomes a commitment. The stalled beat, the question that unsticks it, and the conversation it is for, role only. Build the card and copy it somewhere you will see it before your next 1:1. Quiet room, go.
facilitator.closeSay: You did the thing this month keeps asking for: you coached, out loud, with witnesses. The weekly sessions carry the theme on: Manager Monday tunes your ear for the coaching moment inside ordinary 1:1s, Take-Off Tuesday puts the growth you coach on the record in Oracle, and Thrive Thursday builds the listening underneath every beat you ran today. If you want the theory behind your reps, this month's LinkedIn Learning pick is Sara Canaday's Coaching Skills for Leaders and Managers; a companion when you are curious, never an assignment. The rep on your card is the only thing due.

contingencies.if: The projector or room screen fails
contingencies.then: The deck lives on learner phones via the welcome QR, and the interactions run there too; narrate from your own device. Triads need chairs, not screens.

contingencies.if: The headcount does not divide into threes
contingencies.then: Run one or two pairs with a navigator as their observer, or a four-seat triad with two observers comparing notes; two observers disagreeing is a debrief gift.

contingencies.if: A coachee's topic turns out to be about a named colleague or a live conflict
contingencies.then: Protect the room warmly: 'Roles, never names.' Reshape the topic toward the coachee's own next move; if it is genuinely hot, swap in their backup topic and offer a navigator conversation afterward.

contingencies.if: A coach freezes mid-round in front of their observer
contingencies.then: Normalize it loudly enough for nearby triads to hear: freezing is the stall showing up on schedule. Feed them one stem, what have you tried, and let the round continue; the recovery is better practice than a smooth round.

toughQuestions.q: My team brings me fires, not coaching topics. When would I ever use this?
toughQuestions.a: Fires need telling, and most fires are the tenth repeat of something coachable. The beats fit inside an ordinary 1:1: the stuck they brought is the topic, and the will with a date is what stops it coming back.

toughQuestions.q: Isn't role-play artificial? People perform instead of coaching.
toughQuestions.a: That is why the practicum runs on brought topics instead of scripts. The coachee wants real movement on a real stuck, so the conversation stops being a performance the moment the first honest answer lands. Ask anyone whose round stopped feeling like practice.

toughQuestions.q: What do I do with my observer notes about someone else's coaching?
toughQuestions.a: Hand them to the coach and let them go; the notes belong to the person they mirror. What you keep is what observing taught your own ear. Nothing from a triad, topics included, travels beyond it, and roles-never-names applies afterward too.

templates.title: Pre-work invite (paste into the calendar invite)
templates.body: Subject: The GROW coaching practicum, in person. Bring one real work topic you want movement on, something stuck this month, described without names. You will coach, be coached, and observe, and you will leave knowing which beat of your coaching stalls. Wear your listening.

templates.title: 7-day pulse (send one week after)
templates.body: Subject: Did the rep happen? Three lines, reply whenever: 1) Did the coaching rep on your card happen? 2) What did the person figure out without being told? 3) Which beat is your next practice?
